title: Communication, behavioral & cases | Emerging frontier topics
objectives: Turn your fintech year into compelling stories. Get a working map of what is new at the frontier.
exercise: Write 6 STAR stories (impact, failure, conflict, ambiguity, leadership, learning) and record 2 of them. Then write a one-page capstone proposal covering the problem, data, eval plan and experiment plan.
resources: CME 295 later lectures (reasoning, RAG, tool calling)

units.title: STAR with metrics
units.concepts: Situation, Task, Action, Result; impact framing

units.title: Reasoning models
units.concepts: Test-time compute, when it's worth paying for

units.title: Responsible AI in finance

cards.q: Rewrite 'I built a model' into an impact statement.
cards.answer: Example: 'I built a transaction-risk model that cut manual fraud reviews by 30% while holding chargeback losses flat, saving ~2 analyst FTEs; I validated it with a 4-week holdout test.'

cards.q: Order the STAR framework.
Which part of a STAR answer should take the most time?
choices: Action (what you did and why), followed by a quantified Result

cards.q: In a failure story, interviewers mainly look for…
choices: Ownership, what you learned, and what you changed afterwards
A story with no real failure

cards.q: Your project's impact is hard to quantify. Best approach?
choices: Give the best defensible estimate or proxy (time saved, decisions changed, risk reduced) and say how you estimated it

cards.q: How do you explain a non-significant result with a positive point estimate to a PM?
cards.answer: 'Our best estimate is +1.5%, but the plausible range is −0.5% to +3.5%. The data can't rule out zero or a small negative effect. We can't confidently say it helps.' Then recommend: extend or re-run with more power if the upside matters, ship if the cost is low and the downside is bounded, or move on. Avoid 'trending positive' and 'almost significant'.
rubric: Uses the interval / range, not just the point estimate
Clear that zero (or negative) is plausible
Gives a decision recommendation with rationale

cards.q: Best structure for an executive take-home or write-up?
choices: Recommendation first, then key evidence, then caveats and details

cards.q: An exec asks 'Is it significant or not?'. Best reply style?
choices: Answer in business terms: likely effect range and what decision it supports

cards.q: Which phrasing is most accurate?
A chart for executives should…
choices: Make one point, with a headline stating the takeaway

cards.q: Outline a story where data changed a stakeholder's mind.
cards.answer: S: a PM wanted to launch X based on a vivid anecdote or a vanity metric. T: you owned the analysis. A: you aligned on the decision criterion first, ran a quick analysis or test (e.g. segmented data showing the effect only in one cohort, or a cannibalisation check), presented it respectfully with the trade-offs, and proposed an alternative. R: the decision changed (scoped launch or different metric), with a measured outcome and a stronger relationship.

cards.q: Grab's '4H' values are…
The data supports the PM's opponent, but the PM is senior and insistent. Best behaviour?
choices: State the evidence and the risk clearly, propose a test or guardrail, and disagree-and-commit if overruled while documenting it

cards.q: 'Googleyness' interviews assess things like…
choices: Comfort with ambiguity, collaboration, intellectual humility and doing the right thing

cards.q: An ambiguity story should show that you…
choices: Structured an unclear problem, made reasonable assumptions explicit, and iterated with stakeholders

cards.q: Balance speed, cost and scale when proposing an incentive experiment at Grab.
cards.answer: Hypothesis: a driver incentive raises supply in peak hours, cutting wait times. Speed: start with a 2-week switchback or geo test in a few cities. Cost: cap budget via a small treatment share and per-driver caps, and estimate cost per incremental trip. Scale: design so the result generalises (representative cities), watch marketplace interference (geo/switchback), and define the go/no-go metric (incremental completed trips per $ with a wait-time guardrail) before rolling out.
rubric: Cost: budget cap / cost per incremental unit

cards.q: Best metric for an incentive's efficiency?
choices: Incremental outcome per dollar (e.g. cost per incremental completed trip)
Number of drivers who received the incentive

cards.q: In a case study, why state hypotheses before diving into data?
choices: It focuses the analysis and shows structured thinking under time pressure

cards.q: A promo boosts orders 20% during the test, but merchants complain of overload. Which dimension did you miss?
choices: Supply-side guardrails (merchant capacity, prep time) in a two-sided marketplace

cards.q: Leadership asks for a quick answer by Friday, but a clean experiment takes 4 weeks. Best move?
choices: Give a directional answer from existing data (with caveats) now, and propose the experiment for a confident decision
Run a 3-day test and present it as conclusive

cards.q: What is test-time compute, and when is it worth paying for?
cards.answer: Spending more inference computation per query (longer reasoning chains, multiple samples with voting/verification, search) to improve answer quality. It's worth it for hard, multi-step, high-value tasks where accuracy matters more than latency and cost: complex analysis, maths, code, planning. It's not worth it for simple lookups, classification or latency-critical paths.
rubric: More inference compute per query (reasoning / sampling)
Worth it: hard, high-value, verifiable tasks
Not worth it: simple or latency-sensitive tasks

cards.q: Self-consistency improves accuracy by…
choices: Sampling several reasoning paths and taking the majority answer

cards.q: Using a reasoning model to classify 1M transaction descriptions is usually…
choices: Poor value: a smaller, cheaper model (or fine-tune) suffices for a simple task

cards.q: A reasoning budget (e.g. max thinking tokens) lets you…
choices: Trade off accuracy against latency and cost per request

cards.q: Why do reasoning models benefit from RL on verifiable tasks?
choices: Automatic correctness checks give a reward signal at scale without human labels

cards.q: Name two checks before trusting agent-written analysis code.
cards.answer: Read and run it yourself on a small known case with an expected answer. Check joins and row counts (no fan-out or duplication), filters and date ranges, null handling, and metric definitions against the source of truth. Reproduce a headline number independently, add assertions/tests, and check that it didn't silently drop errors or use made-up columns.
rubric: Any two of: known-answer test, row-count/join checks, definition check, independent reproduction, assertions

cards.q: Most dangerous failure of AI-written SQL analysis?
choices: Plausible-looking numbers from a subtly wrong join or filter that runs without error

cards.q: Give a coding agent which database access for exploratory analysis?
choices: Read-only, on a non-production replica, with row and time limits

cards.q: Best use of coding agents in a DS workflow?
choices: Speeding up boilerplate, plotting and refactoring, with you verifying logic and conclusions

cards.q: An agent reports a 40% lift. Twyman's law suggests…
choices: Be suspicious and verify the pipeline before sharing
It must be right because code ran

cards.q: Give one fintech use case where OCR-free document models help.
cards.answer: KYC: extracting fields from ID cards and proof-of-address documents with varied layouts. Receipt or invoice parsing for expense or merchant onboarding. Bank statement understanding for credit underwriting. Vision-language models read layout, tables and stamps directly, without brittle OCR → regex pipelines.

cards.q: Main advantage of vision-language models over OCR + rules for documents?
choices: They use layout and visual context, generalising across templates without hand-written rules

cards.q: Key risk when using document AI for KYC?
choices: Hallucinated or misread fields accepted without verification; need confidence thresholds and human review

cards.q: How should you evaluate a receipt-extraction model?
choices: Field-level accuracy on a labelled set spanning merchants, languages, image quality

cards.q: Multimodal models process images by…
choices: Encoding image patches into embeddings the language model attends to alongside text tokens

cards.q: Why do lending models face stricter explainability requirements?
choices: Credit decisions significantly affect people and are regulated: applicants are often owed reasons for adverse decisions, and lenders must show they don't discriminate

cards.q: Removing 'race' from features guarantees fairness?
choices: No: proxies (postcode, names, spending) can encode it; measure outcomes across groups

cards.q: Synthetic data risk for training a fraud model?
choices: It may miss real-world edge cases and amplify generator biases, inflating offline metrics
It's always better than real data
It can't be used at all
It removes the need for evals

cards.q: Privacy-preserving practice for LLM apps handling customer data?
choices: Minimise and redact PII before sending it to models, apply access controls and retention limits, and check vendor data terms

cards.q: Two fairness criteria often in tension?
choices: Equal false-positive/negative rates across groups vs calibration within groups (when base rates differ)
